Drivers are actually one of the strength of linux....you hardly ever have to bother yourself with them. Usually things just work..you don't have to install drivers at all. There are two exceptions from this though...wifi and graphics cards.

In the wifi case it's because most wifi dongles needs some proprietary firmware uploaded to them at start....and that is usually not included in the default configuration of linux distros or not available at all. So for wifi check the web first if you adapter is supported or grab a live distro and try it out before getting disappointed later.

The graphics card case is a bit different...the main reason here is that there are too many drivers ;). Distros usually install the open source drivers which is fine for AMD and intel based graphics boards but not so much for nvidia. There you probably want the proprietary drivers from nvidia. But distros usually have instructions on their websites how to install those.

Just one thing you need to keep in mind with drivers in linux..it works the same as with programs. You never download them yourself but rather use the package manager to install them. Linux is not windows.

Well..games...work but yeah, you are right...it's not the primary use-case for linux. As a pure gaming system you are better off with windows most likely.

Not every need someone might have in the art sector can be fulfilled...but a lot can. You have to decide if that available programs are enough for you.

I've used Linux as my only OS for years (my distro of choice has been Sabayon for most of them). I use it primarily for browsing, programming and gaming (between WINE and native ports, everything I've wanted to play has been available). I use Nvidia cards with the proprietary drivers, and haven't had any major issues (the worst was some slight graphical corruption on a third screen until I forced a repaint). Some games (especially WINE ones) have required a little tinkering (usually just reading the appdb page and following the instructions), but they generally work as expected.

Just recently I re-built my system as a multiseat gaming gig, so that my gf and I can game on it simultaneously - from a user's perspective it's like having two separate PCs, but there's only one set of hardware (need individual graphics cards though). It works brilliantly, and ended up being significantly cheaper than two separate PCs.

I should add that Sabayon is an excellent distro for gaming and the like, as it's one of the few distros to ship the proprietary drivers by default; I haven't had to worry about them once when using it. (It was also one of the first to add bumblebee and UEFI support.) It's a (near) bleeding edge rolling release distro though, so while it's been pretty stable in my experience, it might not be for everyone.

One thing you might want to consider is running a hybrid environment, running one OS in a VM and the other natively. I don't know how easy it would be to use PCIe passthrough for a virtualized Windows, or whether the benefits of having a second OS would be worth it, but you could probably get the best of both worlds that way. (At the very least, it could serve as a gateway drug.)
